To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

children's clandestine reading practice is an ideologically grounded activity that is organized by the institutionalized norms of reading and that is enacted by children who are aware of and sensitive to these norms.
children’s clandestine practice of reading is an instance of interactional reading, and that interactional reading is an example of double-voicing.
children's interactional reading practice is a form of clandestine reading that involves the use of intertextuality and double- voicing.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the way in which children's reading practices are organized in relation to the institutional context in which they occur, and with the way in that reading practice is a social activity, a social process that is always embedded in a social context.
how the clandestine practice of reading unfolds in the school classroom.
how the habitus of the institutionally prescribed way of reading is reproduced, and how it is also transformed by children's clandestine interactional practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
clandestine interactional reading constitutes a subaltern form of reading that is both enabled and constrained by its institutionalized counterpart, the normative reading practice of the classroom.
the article contributes to the study of reading as an ideological practice, as well as to the study of clandestine reading as a form of double-voicing.
clandestine interactional reading is an act of double-voicing that allows children to engage in a practice of reading that is at once a subversive act and a means for them to learn how to read.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a theoretical model for the study of reading as an interactional practice and a method for its analysis.
the article contributes to the understanding of reading as a practice that is embedded in the cultural, institutional, and ideological contexts in which it is carried out.
this article approaches clandestine reading as a form of intertextuality that is produced in the interstices of the institutionalized reading practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reading is a complex and multilayered activity that cannot be reduced to the mere act of decoding the written word.

children's interactional reading is not only an alternative form of text access and meaning-making; it is also a form of social action that challenges the hegemonic reading canon and the institutionalized reading regime that sustains it.
children are not only active agents of change but also the agents of the reproduction of the norm.
